parts.label: Part 4
parts.article:
Part four.

You will hear part of a lecture about a Japanese museum comprised mainly of underground space. First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

For the last few sessions, we've been looking at the different architecture for both their utilitarian purposes and aesthetic features as well. In today's lecture, I want to continue this series by first introducing to you a unique underground museum in Japan, and then we'll discuss the pros and cons of underground architecture.

Now, this museum was built in nineteen ninety-six, and around eighty percent of the museum is buried underground to preserve the lush natural beauty. It houses an impressive collection of artworks. The exhibits consist of works from ancient civilizations, including the Egyptians, Romans, and various Asian cultures, with the pieces mainly coming from the founder's private collection.

But perhaps the most intriguing aspect of the museum is the design of its structures and how they are integrated into their natural surroundings. The museum is humbly embedded in mountains close to a subway station connecting the nearest metropolis in about an hour.

The design was inspired by an ancient Chinese story titled Peach Blossom Valley. The architect read it when he was a schoolboy. It is about a fisherman who loses his way and his boat carries him upstream. He is drawn into a cave by the fragrant scent of a forest of blossoming peach trees. After traveling through a narrow road behind the cave, the man finds an idyllic village amid the splendid view. The museum has been conceived as a real-world version of this village. Visitors must pass through a tunnel first and then a cable bridge suspended over a gorge before arriving at the museum.

The museum's details reflect the designer's innovative endeavor to break new ground. The architect changed the design numerous times to ensure the building was in harmony with the natural landscape. It becomes evident as tourists walk around the building as the detail is very fastidious and makes for a unique experience. Once visitors enter the museum, a sloping roof made of wide expanses of glass draws their attention right away. The web-like structure filtered the light through and scattered it across the surface, making visitors feel like being outside with a vibrant backdrop of seasonal colors.

It is now clear that underground buildings have many advantages over traditional above ground houses. And many architects are looking into the possibilities of this type of subsurface structure. The most important advantage of these houses, especially in the current scenario of environmental degradation, is that they can better preserve indigenous flora and fauna. But the advantages of underground architecture go beyond that.

For one thing, the earth surrounding the homes absorbs noise and thus provides natural soundproofing, creating a quiet living space with privacy. Choosing an underground house will be peaceful and calming even in a noisy region.

Moreover, there is less part of underground houses that can catch fire. For the most part, wood is no longer needed for building a home underground. The concrete foundations and metal structures of these homes all ensure good fireproofing.

Now underground houses also have the potential to save energy in the long run as they can tap the earth's heating or cooling power. The earth's temperature doesn't vary as much as the temperature of the air outside. It ensures that even though the climate outside fluctuates between extremes, the conditions inside the subterranean homes remain more or less stable

However, there are also concerns over earth-sheltered homes. There may be a psychological adjustment needed for a person shifting from a traditional above-ground house to an underground house. Many people feel there is insufficient space in underground buildings. But in fact, these people also admit that they often visit shopping centers located in the basement and did not feel claustrophobic.

In addition, underground houses cannot be built in regions experiencing flooding due to their unique geographical location. And even for areas that are suited for underground structures, drainage should be planned carefully to prevent moisture retention.

While the advantages far outnumber their drawbacks, it may be a good idea to wait a little longer for these houses to come mainstream.

That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

analyses.content: 录音中提到博物馆谦虚地“嵌入在山中（embedded in mountains）”，这里的 embedded in 完美对应题目中的“被...环绕（surrounded by）”。
你可能会听到后面的 subway station 或者 metropolis，但这些是靠近的地标或连接的目的地，而不是“环绕”博物馆的自然背景词。

But perhaps the most intriguing aspect of the museum is the design of its structures and how they are integrated into their natural surroundings. The museum is humbly embedded in mountains close to a subway station, connecting the nearest metropolis in about an hour.
录音明确说到设计灵感来源于一个中国的古老故事（ancient Chinese story），并且建筑师在学生时代读过它，对应题目的 the architect knew。
你可能会听到 Peach Blossom Valley（桃花源），但这只是故事的具体名字，填进去超过了题目“ONE WORD ONLY”的数量限制。
The design was inspired by an ancient Chinese story titled Peach Blossom Valley. The architect read it when he was a schoolboy.
录音明确给出了先后顺序，游客必须先穿过一个隧道（pass through a tunnel），然后再走过吊桥，对应题目中的 approach...through a ___ and over a bridge。
你可能会听到 gorge（峡谷），但那是桥悬挂在上方的地方，而不是游客直接“穿过（through）”的通道结构。
Visitors must pass through a tunnel first and then a cable bridge suspended over a gorge before arriving at the museum.
录音中说到游客一旦进入博物馆，由大片玻璃制成的倾斜屋顶（sloping roof）会立刻吸引他们的注意，对应题目中的 a glass ___ can be noticed immediately。
题目限定了材质是 glass（玻璃），录音里修饰玻璃的实体核心词是 roof（屋顶），你不要只顾着听玻璃而漏听了它到底是个什么建筑结构。
Once visitors enter the museum, a sloping roof made of wide expanses of glass draws their attention right away.
录音提到网状结构让光线透过来并散布开，让游客感觉像是在“外面（feel like being outside）”。
这里的考点是光线带来的“感受”，你不要被紧接着出现的补充背景词 seasonal colors（季节色彩）转移了注意力而填错。
The web-like structure filtered the light through and scattered it across the surface, making visitors feel like being outside with a vibrant backdrop of seasonal colors.
录音提到泥土吸收噪音（absorbs noise），从而提供自然的隔音效果，对应题目中地下建筑的优势：“更少的...（less）”。
你可能会顺手写下 soundproofing，但这是提供的好处（隔音），被减少/吸收的对象本身是 noise（噪音）。
For one thing, the earth surrounding the homes absorbs noise and thus provides natural soundproofing, creating a quiet living space with privacy.
录音直接说明，地下房屋能着火（catch fire）的部分更少，完美对应题目里的“处于较低的火灾风险中（lower risk of fire）”。
你可能会被后面跟读的 wood（木头）干扰，但录音的意思是“不再需要木头”，作为风险点填在这里语义完全不对。
Moreover, there is less part of underground houses that can catch fire.
录音指出，许多人觉得地下建筑里的空间不足（insufficient space），对应题目中地下建筑的缺点：“not have enough...”。
前面提到了 psychological adjustment（心理调整），但那只是一个宽泛的引入句，真正在具体抱怨“不够”的东西是 space。

There may be a psychological adjustment needed for a person shifting from a traditional above-ground house to an underground house. Many people feel there is insufficient space in underground buildings.
录音里说，其实这些人也承认，他们经常去位于地下室（located in the basement）的购物中心，并不觉得难受。
题目的定位词是 shopping centres，你需要抓取修饰这个词的具体位置信息，不要填成后面的生僻形容词 claustrophobic（幽闭恐惧的）。
But in fact, these people also admit that they often visit shopping centers located in the basement and did not feel claustrophobic.
录音明确表示，由于特殊的地理位置，地下房屋不能建在经历洪水（experiencing flooding）的地区，experiencing 同义替换题目的 suffering from。
只要你听懂“cannot be built”这个关键的否定限定词，紧跟在后面的就是答案所在，不要被稍后的 geographical location 扰乱节奏。
In addition, underground houses cannot be built in regions experiencing flooding due to their unique geographical location.
